title: Restates the formula
statement: How many positive integers $n$ are such that $n + 30$ divides $n^2 + 300$?
hints: Compare $n$ with $n + 30$: what is $n^2 + 300$ close to?
Reduce modulo $n + 30$: the remainder is a constant, so $n + 30$ must be one of its divisors above $30$.
solution: Since $n \equiv -30 \pmod{n+30}$, we have $n^2 + 300 \equiv 900 + 300 = 1200 \pmod{n+30}$. So the condition is that $n + 30$ divides $1200$, with $n + 30 > 30$. The number $1200 = 2^4\cdot 3\cdot 5^2$ has $5\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 30$ divisors. They pair up as $d \cdot (1200/d)$. Those at most $30$ are $1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,15,16,20,24,25,30$, which is $15$ divisors, leaving $15$ above $30$. So there are $15$ values of $n$. Why this works. divisor-counting: reducing modulo the divisor leaves a constant, whose divisors can be counted.
